transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-01-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Arjun Reddy (Redwood CSM), Sahar Patel (Orion Head of ML), Tom Rivera (Orion Infra), Priya Menon (Orion CTO)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, error analysis, request logs and debugging flows. Focus on how to triage high-latency requests and data retention/security controls for pilot.

00:00 Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, happy New Year. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Miguel our solutions engineer and Arjun from customer success. We'll run through the Console tracing, error analysis, request logs and a couple debugging flows.
00:18 Miguel: Hi all, Miguel here. I'll share my screen in a sec. Quick note, we're gonna show both the UI flows and a short demo of capturing a live request and stepping through the KV cache and kernel selection traces.
00:33 Sahar: Great, thanks. Our main goals today are to understand how we'd debug model timeouts, where we can see token-level latency, and what logs we get for PII filtering. Also curious about on-prem options and VPC connectivity.
00:48 Tom: Also, retention — we have compliance requirements for 7 years for certain logs, so we need to know export and storage options.
00:56 Miguel: Understood. We'll cover tracing span details, request logs retention and export, and redaction controls. I'll start with the Console.
01:10 Miguel: (screen) So this is the Console main dashboard. On the left you can see Routes, Models, Traces, and Request Logs. We'll open Traces.
01:22 Miguel: The Traces view groups by request id, you can filter by model version, route, and timeframe. Here I'm selecting a trace — the single-request flame shows steps: auth, routing, batching, model exec, kernel selection, kv-cache hit/miss.
01:41 Lena: A quick note — terms may show slightly different in the UI, sometimes auto-transcripts write K-V cash instead of KV cache.
01:48 Sahar: (laugh) yeah we saw that in the doc. Are the kernel names and GPU IDs exposed? We need to tie slow requests back to infra.
01:58 Miguel: Yes, you can see kernel selection metadata and instance id. We show host id and region, though host names are masked unless you opt into more verbose logs.
02:10 Miguel: Here's an example trace where latency spikes on model exec. If you expand the model exec span you get token-level timing and cumulative token times, and you can export that as a CSV for offline analysis.
02:28 Tom: Token-level timing — is that per-token or per-batch?
02:34 Miguel: Per-token within the model exec span; we also show batch composition so you can see how a request was grouped. That helps identify bad batching patterns causing tail latency.
02:47 Sahar: Does the Console indicate when a request was served from cache vs generating new tokens?
02:51 Miguel: Yep, kv-cache spans show hit/miss and prefix length. We also surface prefix cache policies — LRU, TTLs. Right now our sample trace shows a cache hit for the first 32 tokens and then a miss.
03:04 Priya: For our legal team, can sensitive content be redacted before logs are stored?
03:09 Miguel: There are built-in redaction hooks. You can apply PII filters server-side and we also support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest. Redaction runs before logs are persisted, though you can configure raw log export to a private bucket if you need to keep full data under your own controls.
03:26 Lena: I'll drop the SOC2 and network diagram in the follow-up.
03:31 Miguel: Moving to Error Analysis — this dashboard aggregates error rates by route and model version. If you click into an error cluster you'll see sample request payloads, stack traces, and correlated traces. Sometimes transcription misses some of these names in the exported text — so you'll see quirks like Redwood-> Red wood in auto transcripts.
03:51 Miguel: Example: a timeout error cluster — the error view links directly to the trace where you can see the tail latency spikes and the kernel fallback to a lower precision implementation.
04:08 Tom: Kernel fallback — does that happen automatically? We don't want precision drops without notice.
04:13 Miguel: Fallbacks are policy-driven. You can configure automatic fallbacks for availability vs strict SLOs. For customers requiring fixed output quality we recommend disabling fallback and instead using canary routes for testing.
04:27 Sahar: We might want fallback only during DR scenarios.
04:30 Miguel: Totally reasonable. You can set fallback triggers based on model exec time, node health or region availability.
04:38 Miguel: Now Request Logs — here you can query requests with filters like route, model, user_id, and custom tags. Each log entry links to a trace, and we've added a quick comparison view to diff two requests side-by-side.
04:56 Priya: About exports: can we stream these logs to our SIEM?
05:00 Miguel: Yes, we support streaming via Kafka or pushing to a customer S3/GCS bucket. For SIEM integrations we can emit to your Splunk/Datadog agents.
05:10 Tom: For retention — if we need 7 years, that's a lot of storage. Any tiered storage options?
05:15 Miguel: We have cold storage export options and compressed archival exports to your bucket. We don't store seven-year data on the hot Console by default—it's exported and archived.
05:25 Sahar: Ok good. Could you show a debugging flow where a request returns an unexpected hallucination and we trace back to training prompts or model version?
05:33 Miguel: Sure — I'll search for a recent request with high hallucination score from our eval hooks.
05:40 Miguel: (navigates) Here's the request, hallucination tag = 0.72, we can see the prompt, the embeddings call, and the model answer. The trace shows an embedding rerank step — that's where we suspect the issue.
05:54 Miguel: You can replay the call in a sandboxed environment with the same route and model version; the Console will spin up a ephemeral repro with identical model artifacts to reproduce deterministically.
06:06 Sahar: Replay is great. Are there limits on replay execution?
06:10 Miguel: For pilot customers we provide a quota for replays; for enterprise there's an admin quota config. Replays don't hit customer billing but count against reserved compute in Dedicated deployments.
06:22 Tom: On network, can we restrict Console access to our SSO?
06:27 Lena: Yes, we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and SCIM provisioning. We'll include the SSO doc.
06:34 Priya: For Private deployments we need the control plane in our VPC, and the inference plane on-prem. How much overlap exists with the hosted Console features?
06:43 Miguel: The Private control plane exposes almost all Console features, tracing and request logs included. There are a few hosted-only integrations (managed analytics export) but core debugging flows are identical.
06:55 Sahar: Any differences in log retention behavior for Private?
06:58 Miguel: You manage retention in Private — you control the storage, retention policies, and encryption keys.
07:07 Miguel: A quick demo: I'll trigger a synthetic request that times out and show how we triage.
07:14 Miguel: (runs) You can see the trace: auth latency normal, routing normal, model exec spikes around token 22, kernel fallback then error. The error analysis flagged it as a timeout with increased CPU steal on the host.
07:33 Tom: CPU steal? That sounds like noisy neighbor. Do you surface host-level metrics?
07:38 Miguel: Yes, host metrics and container metrics are correlated in the trace view; we show CPU, memory, GPU util, and kernel latency histograms. For Dedicated customers you can opt into host-level telemetry.
07:50 Sahar: For our compliance audit they'd want immutable logs with signatures. Does Redwood support signed exports?
07:57 Lena: We support signed exports to your S3 with customer-managed KMS; we can add object-level signatures in the export pipeline. I'll confirm exact format in the follow-up.
08:09 Priya: Regarding throughput, we typically send 2K requests/second during peak. Any rule of thumb for batching to keep within SLOs?
08:17 Miguel: We recommend route-level batching configs; for 2K rps you want to prefer smaller max batch sizes with dynamic batching tuned to latency SLOs. Our Optimize product can suggest batching profiles based on historic traces.
08:34 Sahar: Does Optimize integrate into Console?
08:37 Miguel: Yes, Optimize suggestions appear as recommendations in the Route config page — quantization, batching, and model variant hints.
08:44 Miguel: Back to the log export, I'll show how to create a pipeline: create export target -> add filters -> opt for raw vs redacted -> schedule daily export.
08:58 Miguel: (clicks) You can also run ad-hoc exports for audit requests; they produce a checksumed tarball for integrity.
09:10 Tom: How are request ids correlated to our internal user ids?
09:14 Miguel: We support custom tags in the request header; you can attach user_id, session_id, or feature flags, and they show up in the request log. We recommend hashing PII before sending to avoid storing raw identifiers.
09:28 Sahar: Ok. For the pilot, we want to run a benchmark of 10k token average request to see tail latencies. Can Redwood run that or do we need to send sample load scripts?
09:37 Miguel: We can run it in partnership — Miguel: We'll provision a test tenant and run the benchmark with your sample prompts.
09:44 Lena: Next steps recap: we'll share SOC2 + SSO doc, Miguel will provision tenant and run 10k-token bench, and Orion will share sample logs.
09:56 Priya: Sounds good. Also please include pricing for Dedicated vs hosted for our projected 2K rps.
10:02 Lena: We'll include pilot pricing and a cost estimate in the follow-up.
10:06 Sahar: One quick question, competitor comparison — we're evaluating Anthropic and OpenAI too. How does Redwood help on cost visibility?
10:15 Lena: Console has token-level cost breakdowns and per-route spend dashboards, and Optimize gives quantization recommendations to save cost. We'll add a cost model for your workload in the pilot.
10:28 Tom: Anything else on security?
10:31 Miguel: We support SOC2, ISO, audit logs, SAML, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. You can restrict export targets to your VPC or private bucket.
10:42 Priya: Perfect.
10:44 Lena: Alright we'll wrap up. Thanks everyone.
